extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy and economic history
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook excerpt outlining aims of political economy and critiquing the mercantile (commercial) system versus an agricultural system; explains causal effects of commerce and manufactures on agriculture, social order, and public revenue. Useful for readers learning foundational distinctions and policy implications in 18th-century political economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of political economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Political economy... proposes two distinct objects; first, to provide a plentiful revenue or subsistence for the people, or, more properly, to enable them to provide such a revenue or subsistence for themselves; and, secondly, to supply the state or commonwealth with a revenue sufficient for the public services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discipline aims to enrich both the people (by enabling self-subsistence/prosperity) and the sovereign (by supplying public revenue). This dual aim frames subsequent distinctions between systems of political economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two systems of political economy: commerce vs agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: The different progress of opulence in different ages and nations, has given occasion to two different systems of political economy, with regard to enriching the people. The one may be called the system of commerce, the other that of agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are distinct approaches to achieving the first object (people's subsistence). The author will explain both systems and notes the commerce-based system is the modern one and best understood in his country and times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantile principle: wealth consists in money (popular notion)
rubrics_metrics.description: That wealth consists in money, or in gold and silver, is a popular notion which naturally arises from the double function of money, as the instrument of commerce, and as the measure of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why contemporaries equate national richness with hoarded specie: money eases exchange and measures value. Examples given: Spaniards seeking gold in newly encountered lands; Tartars assessing wealth by cattle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique: real wealth is consumable goods, not merely specie
rubrics_metrics.description: Others admit, that if a nation could be separated from all the world... the real wealth or poverty of the country... would depend altogether upon the abundance or scarcity of those consumable goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an isolated economy, consumable goods constitute true wealth; specie is less relevant. Even for nations with foreign connections, accumulation of gold/silver is precarious because specie can be exported and capital moved; real, durable wealth is secured when capital is realized in lasting domestic improvements (buildings, cultivated land).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locke's distinction between money and other moveable goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr Locke remarks a distinction between money and other moveable goods. All other moveable goods... are of so consumable a nature, that the wealth which consists in them cannot be much depended on;... Money, on the contrary, is a steady friend...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This argument supports why contemporaries prize specie: money is less likely to be consumed away, whereas consumables can be wasted. But the chapter balances this with the observation that money's steadiness matters less for isolated economies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and manufactures promote agricultural improvement and markets
rubrics_metrics.description: To all of them they afforded a market for some part either of their rude or manufactured produce... Secondly, the wealth acquired by the inhabitants of cities was frequently employed in purchasing such lands as were to be sold... Merchants are commonly ambitious of becoming country gentlemen, and, when they do, they are generally the best of all improvers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commerce creates local markets that encourage production and improvement; merchant habits (order, economy, profit-seeking) make them effective at investing in land improvement, often more so than traditional country gentlemen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and manufactures induce order, liberty, and security
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, and lastly, commerce and manufactures gradually introduced order and good government, and with them the liberty and security of individuals... This, though it has been the least observed, is by far the most important of all their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By reducing dependence on great proprietors (who once maintained retainers and tenants at will), commerce undermines feudal power structures and fosters regular government, individual security, and diminished private coercive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital acquired by commerce is precarious until realized in lasting improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital, however, that is acquired to any country by commerce and manufactures, is always a very precarious and uncertain possession, till some part of it has been secured and realized in the cultivation and improvement of its lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchant capital can be moved between countries; it only becomes durable national wealth when invested in immovable or lasting domestic assets (buildings, improved land). Historical examples given (Hanse towns, decline of commerce) illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property structure and small proprietors encourage improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A small proprietor, who knows every part of his little territory, views it with all the affection which property, especially small property, naturally inspires... is generally of all improvers the most industrious, the most intelligent, and the most successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and customs that concentrate land (primogeniture, perpetuities) hinder the multiplication of small proprietors and therefore slow agricultural improvement. In colonies where land is cheap and purchasable, small capital can be profitably employed in cultivation and rapid development occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy instruments that favor agriculture (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of England... Except in times of scarcity, the exportation of corn is not only free, but encouraged by a bounty. In times of moderate plenty, the importation of foreign corn is loaded with duties that amount to a prohibition. The importation of live cattle, except from Ireland, is prohibited at all times...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These legal measures give cultivators a domestic monopoly on staple produce (bread and butcher’s meat) and provide direct encouragements to agriculture; combined with legal security for yeomanry (tenure protections), they aim to favor agricultural industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social effects of spending rents on tradesmen versus retainers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the great proprietors of land spend their rents in maintaining their tenants and retainers, each of them maintains entirely all his own tenants and all his own retainers. But when they spend them in maintaining tradesmen and artificers... Each tradesman or artificer derives his subsistence from the employment, not of one, but of a hundred or a thousand different customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spending on manufactured goods disperses dependence: craftsmen rely on many customers and are not absolutely dependent on any single patron, which reduces the personal power of great proprietors, leads to dismissal of retainers, and fosters independent tenants and regular governance.
